title: AI Coding is exhausting
summary: A short reflective video on why AI-assisted coding leaves developers mentally drained. Matt Pocock explains that coding used to alternate between strategic thinking and tactical implementation - and the tactical part (writing the code, moving things around, almost like playing a game) functioned as a break for the brain. AI has eaten that tactical side entirely, so now every working moment is strategic, long-term thinking. Developers must operate one level above the AI, reviewing and directing instead of doing - everyone has effectively been promoted to lead developer. That elevation demands high-level decision-making all day, which is rewarding but exhausting: he ends each day knackered and says this shift is baked into the loaf for anyone using AI.
what_you_learn: You get a framework for what your role becomes when AI does the implementation: the tactical work disappears, and your job is continuous strategic direction one level above the agent. Understanding this shift - and that the fatigue is structural, not a personal failing - helps you design sustainable workflows around agentic tools instead of burning out on them.

skills.name: Strategic Thinking
skills.description: With AI handling implementation, all remaining developer work is long-term strategic reasoning.

skills.name: Human-in-the-Loop Collaboration
skills.description: Removing grunt work does not remove strain - it concentrates the day into nonstop high-level decisions.

learnings.title: Tactical coding used to be a mental break
learnings.detail: Traditional coding sessions alternated between strategy and implementation. Writing the code was the tactical side - almost non-verbal reasoning, moving stuff around, kind of playing a game - and it gave the brain a rest between hard decisions. That rhythm structured the cognitive load of a dev day.

learnings.title: AI has eaten the tactical side of programming
learnings.detail: Implementation is exactly what AI took over, so the restorative tactical work is gone. Everything that remains in a coding session is strategic, long-term thinking - there is no more downshift available in the workflow. Matt frames this as simply the new reality of AI-assisted development.

learnings.title: You now have to think above the AI's level
learnings.detail: To direct an AI tool usefully you must operate at a level above the one the AI is working at: see the whole picture, anticipate where it will go wrong, and shape the approach before and while it executes. Your attention moves up the abstraction ladder permanently.

learnings.title: Everyone using AI has become a lead developer
learnings.description: Matt's memorable line: we have all turned into lead developers - moved higher up the chain where the job is delegation, review, and direction rather than doing. That is a genuine promotion in responsibility, and it demands the high-level thinking that comes with it.

learnings.title: The strain is structural, not optional
learnings.detail: The trade is explicit: boring grunt work is taken away, but the brain is under much more constant strain, and Matt admits he ends each day pretty knackered even though he enjoys making high-level decisions. He offers no fix - the shift is baked into the loaf for anyone using AI - so the takeaway is to expect and plan for the fatigue, not to feel individually broken by it.

key_points: AI ate the tactical side of programming - the part that used to give your brain a break.
Every developer using AI has been promoted to lead developer, like it or not.
You must think one level above the level the AI is operating at.
Less grunt work does not mean less strain - it means nonstop strategic decisions.
The exhaustion is structural: baked into the loaf, not a personal failure.
